title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Re-opened Applications
shortTitle: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Re-opened Applications
summary: Re-opened applications abuse the macOS logon resume feature, in which applications open at shutdown or log out are recorded and started again at the next login. The list is stored in a property list file named for the login window inside the per-host preferences folder, together with a machine specific identifier. An adversary with user-level access can write an extra entry, or alter an existing entry, so a chosen path is opened automatically when the user next signs in, giving persistence without administrator rights and without a scheduled task or a system daemon. The visible artefact is the property list itself: unexpected application paths, unusual modification times, and entries pointing at binaries in user-writable directories rather than installed applications. Because the mechanism is a normal convenience feature, defenders differentiate malicious entries by comparing the file with an expected baseline, by checking the signature or provenance of each listed path, and by correlating logon-time process creation with the file modification.

beginner.definition: macOS can remember which windows and applications were open and reopen them the next time you sign in. That list is kept in a preference file. An attacker can add a program to the list so it starts when you log in.
beginner.whyItMatters: This trick needs only the rights of a normal user account. It does not need an administrator password or a system service. The behaviour looks exactly like the helpful feature you already use, so nobody becomes suspicious. Because the entry is a harmless-looking path in a settings file, it can survive many logins before anyone notices.
howItWorks: When you log out or restart through the macOS interface, you can tick a box to reopen windows later.
macOS records the open applications in a preference file inside your personal Library folder.
The file name includes a machine identifier, so it is specific to that Mac.
At your next login, macOS reads the list and opens each application it finds.
An attacker edits the list so their own program is among the entries that reopen.
Detection compares the file with a baseline and checks where each listed program actually lives.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel where guests can ask the front desk to wake them with a phone call. The clerk keeps a list of room numbers and times on a clipboard by the phone. Anyone who can reach the clipboard can add a request. At the right hour the clerk politely makes the call, exactly as asked, and the guest never wonders who wrote it down.
takeaways: This persistence needs no administrator rights, so user-level preference files matter for detection.
Check which programs are set to reopen automatically and where those programs live on disk.
Because the file is plain settings, record its normal contents and alert on unexpected changes.

objectives: Explain what the macOS re-open windows feature does and where it stores its list.
Describe how an attacker uses that list to run a program at the next login without administrator rights.
Locate the per-host login window preference file and interpret its entries.
Detect suspicious entries using baseline comparison, file monitoring, and process creation records.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from other macOS logon persistence mechanisms.
Describe why the technique blends in with legitimate user behaviour.
